narrative_purpose: Shows light-enhanced calcification: the same coral lays down skeleton faster in daylight than in darkness, because photosynthesis fuels the process.
subject: A single coral colony shown twice side by side as one continuous scene split by lighting. On the sunlit left half, the polyps are fully extended and bright, and a visibly thick fresh pale rim of new skeleton is forming beneath them. On the dim right half, the same polyps are contracted and dull, and only a thin sliver of new skeleton has formed. A soft gradient of light runs from bright upper-left to dark lower-right across the middle.
scene: One reef ledge under a day-to-night light gradient, clear water, no hard border between the two halves.
camera: Straight-on comparative view at coral scale, the colony centered, left bright and right dim.
light: Warm-tinged bright teal daylight on the left with cyan glow on the fresh skeleton; deep indigo shadow on the right with only faint glow.
palette: Bright ocean teal and cyan on the lit side, void indigo on the dark side, pale skeleton throughout.
style: Painterly naturalist comparison plate, organic light gradient rather than a hard split panel.
detail_level: Crisp on the two skeleton rims (thick vs thin) and polyp states; simple graded background.
composition: Left-bright / right-dim across the frame with open sky-water band above framed by deep negative space contrasting day vs night growth.
consistency_notes: It must read as the SAME colony under two light levels, not two species. Fresh skeleton is clearly thicker on the sunlit side.
negative_prompt: no text, no labels, no arrows, no sun or clock icons, no panel dividers, no photographic or 3D-render look, no cartoon style
